Un tsunami de votos censura las políticas de Trump 
ctxt.es/es/20261101/...

What happened Two years ago, Republicans won the White House and both chambers of Congress. Trump's 2024 coalition had made real gains with Latino and younger voters. On November 3, 2026, all of that reversed. This article explains the midterm inversion using an ancient Chinese idea and a modern scientific theory. Most importantly, it draws a real-life lesson : how to keep the next swing, whenever it comes, from being this violent. Some called it a "blue tsunami." As of November 5, with two Senate races and some House races still being counted: Democrats flipped at least seven Republican Senate seats and took control of the Senate, including Kansas, which hadn't elected a Democratic senator since 1932. Democrats gained more than 40 House seats. CBS projected they would finish with 251 to 268. In Texas, Republicans lost every statewide race on the ballot, ending 32 years of Republican control. Democrats' share of the Latino vote rose from about 55% in 2024 to about 65%, according to Equis. Outgoing Florida governor Ron DeSantis called it "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country." The usual explanations are prices, tariffs, the war with Iran, and a verdict on Trump. Those are the causes . They don't explain the shape . Here is the strange part. Pollsters saw a wave coming. They expected Democrats to win the House vote by about 9 points. Early counts put it closer to 13. Discontent had been building for two years, and then it broke all at once, harder than anyone measured. Why would something build slowly and then break suddenly? Chinese thought has an old answer. Modern mathematics has a newer one. I will show how they fit together to answer this question. This is a simplified version of a more detailed article with deeper mathematical analysis and more in-depth references on the Chinese text. The old answer: 物極必反 物極必反 : when something reaches its extreme, it turns into its opposite. The idea runs through two of the oldest Chinese classics. The Dao De Jing (道德經) says it plainly: 「反者道之動。」 Reversal is how the Dao moves. (ch. 40) 「禍兮福之所倚，福兮禍之所伏。」 Misfortune is what good fortune leans on; good fortune is where misfortune hides. (ch. 58) 「功遂身退，天之道也。」 When the work is done, step back. That is the way of heaven. (ch. 9) The Yi Jing (易經) tells it as a story. The first hexagram, 乾, is six lines of pure yang, read from the bottom up. A dragon rises: first hidden, then appearing in the field, then flying in the sky at the fifth line, 飛龍在天. That is the peak. Then comes the sixth line, the top: 亢龍有悔, the overreaching dragon has regret. The commentary explains why: 「盈不可久也」, fullness cannot last. The dragon at the top knows how to advance but not how to retreat. The second hexagram (in the traditional King Wen order), 坤, is pure yin, and it fails the same way. At its top line, yin pushed to its limit turns and fights: 龍戰于野, dragons battle in the wild. (qian-kun.png) 乾 and 坤, read from the bottom up. The fifth line of 乾 is the best position. The top line of each is where it fails: pure yang overreaches, and pure yin turns and fights. The correspondence to the 2026 midterm is easy to see. A party holding the White House, the Senate and the House is on the top line. Two years later, the reversal came. There is no fixed middle: 時中 People often read Chinese harmony as "stay in the middle and never swing." The classics say something more interesting. The Doctrine of the Mean (中庸) says the wise person practices 時中: the center that fits this moment. The center moves. Mencius warns that holding to the middle without adjusting is no better than holding to an extreme. Zhu Xi (朱熹) put it most simply: 「中無定體，隨時而在」, the mean has no fixed form; it depends on the time. So harmony isn't standing still; it is moving well. A swing back and forth isn't a failure of balance. As long as it stays within bounds, it is the balance. The new answer: why change comes suddenly The Chinese old idea says reversal will come. It doesn't say why it comes all at once. For that, there's a branch of mathematics called catastrophe theory , developed in the 1970s to study things that change smoothly and then suddenly snap. Think of a stiff light switch. You press on it a little: nothing happens. You press harder: still nothing. Then, past a certain point, it snaps to the other side. Your push grew smoothly, but the switch didn't move smoothly at all. It held, and then it flipped. Now notice something else. Once it has flipped, easing off a little doesn't flip it back. You have to push all the way the other way. The switch "remembers" which side it was on. Elections can behave like that switch: The push is pressure on the party in power: prices, an unpopular war, low approval. The stiffness is party loyalty, or polarization. The more loyal voters are, the harder the switch. The switch position is how people vote. When loyalty is strong, voters stick with their side even as pressure builds. Polls barely move. That looks like stability. But it isn't stability; it's a stiff switch under load. When it finally gives, it snaps hard. That is the most useful lesson here: calm on the surface is not proof that you're far from the edge. In 2026, vote intentions shifted only modestly while the underlying pressure was severe. Then it broke. You can try this yourself in an interactive simulator: Drift and Snap . Raise the polarization, push the pressure, and watch the switch hold, then snap. The section "Under the hood: catastrophe theory" near the end explains what each part of the simulator stands for. (fold-boundary.png) Left: the state holds steady while pressure builds, then jumps at the edge (orange arrows). Right: the stronger the loyalty, the wider the gap between where it flips over and where it flips back. Why the reversal keeps coming A stiff switch explains the sudden flip. But what keeps pushing it? Political scientists have noticed that public opinion works like a thermostat. When the government moves one way, the public tends to lean back the other way. The party in power gets blamed for whatever goes wrong: prices, wars, tariffs. So simply holding power builds up pressure against you. Put the two ideas together and you get a cycle: hold power, pressure builds, the switch snaps, the other side holds power, pressure builds against them , and it snaps back. That is 盈不可久 as a mechanism: success creates the conditions for its own reversal. The math adds one more surprise, and it's the strongest point in this whole argument: In a less polarized country , the middle is a stable place to be. Shocks cause swings, but they fade, and politics drifts back toward the center. 執中, holding the middle, works. In a highly polarized country , the middle is no longer stable. The system can't rest there. It swings back and forth on its own, sitting still for a while and then lurching. Only 時中, the moving center, describes it. So polarization doesn't just make swings bigger. It changes what kind of system you have: from a pendulum that settles back to the middle, to one that sits still and then snaps, where a small change in pressure can produce a large jump. What this can't tell us This is a way of seeing the election, not proof: Who voted matters. Part of the swing may be that different people turned out, not that people changed their minds. That isn't a "snap" in anyone's opinion. Midterms usually go against the president. A big loss is not automatically a different kind of event. It can't predict timing. Neither the Yi Jing nor the math tells you when the next flip will come. The Yi Jing's advice is to read the times. The math's advice is to watch the pressure, not just the polls. The dragon, again If this frame is right, it applies to everyone. Two years ago, Republicans held everything. Now Democrats hold Congress, though not the presidency. Polls also show many voters still dislike the Democratic Party, and its edge on the economy is slim. A big win built on the other side's failure is not the same as a mandate. 盈不可久 applies to them too. Now suppose the loop did break, and one party never came back. The cycle wouldn't end. It would move inside the winner. Every coalition has its own poles: among Democrats, democratic socialists and progressives on one side and moderates on the other; among Republicans, the MAGA wing and the old establishment. Take away the outside rival, and the same pressure, the same stiffness and the same snaps play out between factions instead of parties. This has happened before. In the one-party Democratic South, the real elections were the primaries, fought between rival factions of the same party. In Japan, the Liberal Democratic Party governed without a break from 1955 to 1993, and power rotated among its internal factions. This is the dot inside each half of the taiji symbol: 陰中有陽，陽中有陰. Each side carries the seed of its opposite. Win completely, and the opposite reappears inside you. So harmony isn't the absence of swings. Power changing hands is the healthy version of the cycle: 時中 at the scale of a country. The warning sign is swings that keep getting bigger, wherever they happen: between the parties, or inside one. The real-life lesson If this analysis holds, the goal isn't to stop power from changing hands. That's the healthy cycle. The goal is to keep the swings gentle instead of violent. Three things follow: Lower the stiffness. In the model, polarization is what turns gentle swings into snaps. In a less polarized system, shocks fade and politics drifts back toward the middle. Reducing polarization doesn't end the cycle; it changes its shape. Don't overreach. 亢龍有悔. Whoever holds power is building pressure against itself, and a majority that governs as if its mandate were unlimited speeds up its own reversal. 功遂身退. This applies to the new Democratic Congress as much as to the Republicans before it. Watch the pressure, not just the polls. Calm polls can hide a stiff switch under load. What drives polarization is debated. Partisan media and social media, with their bots, trolls and influencers, are often blamed, but the evidence is mixed: polarization rose fastest among older Americans, who use social media least, and large experiments that changed people's Facebook and Instagram feeds during the 2020 election found little effect. Researchers also point to party sorting, cable news, primaries, and where people choose to live. Whatever the causes, the model's point stands: the less polarized a country is, the more gently power changes hands. Under the hood: catastrophe theory Some technical details for readers who want to know what the light switch stands for. Where it comes from Catastrophe theory was created by the French mathematician René Thom in the 1960s and popularized in the 1970s by the British mathematician Christopher Zeeman. "Catastrophe" here doesn't mean disaster. It means a sudden jump in a system whose causes change smoothly. Zeeman applied it to everything from dogs deciding whether to attack or flee to stock market crashes and prison riots. The cusp: one state, two controls The model used here is the simplest interesting one, the cusp catastrophe . It has one thing we watch (the state : how people vote) and two things that drive it (the controls ): The normal factor pushes the state one way or the other. In the switch, it's how hard you press. In the election, it's pressure on the party in power. The splitting factor decides whether the system behaves smoothly or snaps. In the switch, it's the stiffness of the spring. In the election, it's polarization. Picture the possible states as a sheet of paper laid over these two controls. Where the splitting factor is weak, the sheet is smooth: push a little, the state moves a little. Where the splitting factor is strong, the sheet develops a fold , like a pleat in a tablecloth. Inside the fold there are three layers over the same spot: an upper sheet and a lower sheet, which are both stable, and a middle layer folded back under, which is unstable. The system can rest on the top or the bottom, never in the middle. (For the curious: the layers are the solutions of x³ + ax + b = 0, where x is the state, b the normal factor and a the splitting factor. The fold appears when a is negative.) Bifurcations: where the behavior changes A bifurcation is a point where a small change in a control produces a change in the kind of behavior, not just its amount. Two kinds matter here: The fold edge. As pressure builds, the system slides along its sheet toward the edge of the fold. At the edge, that sheet simply ends. The state has nowhere to stand and drops to the other sheet. That's the snap, and it's what happened on election night. The cusp point. The two fold edges start from a single point, where the paper first begins to pleat. On one side of it the system is smooth; on the other, it can snap. This is where polarization first becomes strong enough to matter. The right panel of the second figure shows the fold opening up: the three curves are three levels of polarization, and the gap between the two edges widens as polarization grows. It widens faster than polarization itself. In this model, if the splitting factor doubles, the gap nearly triples. Zeeman's warning signs Zeeman listed five signatures of a cusp catastrophe. Three are visible in elections: Sudden jumps. The state stays nearly put while pressure builds, then jumps. Hysteresis. The jump back happens at a different point than the jump forward. The switch remembers its side. This is why a party that loses voters in a wave doesn't win them back by fixing things just a little. Divergence. Near the cusp point, two situations that start almost the same can end up on opposite sheets. The other two are bimodality (the system tends to be found in one of two states, rarely between them) and inaccessibility (the middle states are unstable, so they're rarely observed). A polarized electorate with a hollowed-out middle shows both. Adding the thermostat: a self-sustaining swing The cusp alone explains the snap but not the cycle. Adding the thermostat (holding power slowly builds pressure against you) turns it into one of the oldest models in physics: the van der Pol oscillator , which Balthasar van der Pol worked out in the 1920s for radio circuits and later used to model the heartbeat. A heartbeat is the right picture: a long quiet build-up, a sudden contraction, then the same again. Here the polarization knob sets a second, deeper bifurcation, called a Hopf bifurcation : Below the threshold , the middle is stable. Shocks cause swings that die down, like a pendulum in honey. Just past the threshold , the middle becomes unstable and the system starts a small, gentle, self-sustaining swing. Deep in polarized territory , the swing turns into long quiet stretches broken by sudden snaps. Physicists call this a relaxation oscillation . This isn't chaos. A chaotic system is unpredictable in principle; this one repeats a regular cycle. The real world adds shocks (wars, scandals, pandemics) that move the timing around, which is why neither the math nor the Yi Jing can tell you when the next snap comes. A fair warning In the 1970s, catastrophe theory was oversold. Critics, including the mathematicians Hector Sussmann and Raphael Zahler, argued that many social-science applications fitted curves after the fact and couldn't be tested. That criticism is fair, and it applies here too. This article uses the cusp as a lens for understanding the shape of what happened, not as a model fitted to election data. Try it yourself The Drift and Snap simulator lets you adjust pressure and polarization and turn the thermostat feedback on and off. Its "Things to try" list walks through each regime: smooth, the switch, drift and snap, and 執中 vs. 時中. Next time What happens when a system has no election to release the pressure? "It’s worth reiterating the obvious: even before this week’s blue tsunami, the AI trade was weakening. And it’s important to recognize just how it was weakening. Initially, tech companies funded the AI buildout with cash. At a certain point, the financing needs grew too big even for companies with hugely positive cash flows, and they started funding the buildout through debt (loans and bonds). In recent weeks, we’ve seen signs that even the debt market won’t be enough, so some companies (like Oracle and Meta) have turned to equity. That also changes the calculation for investors. The AI buildout is no longer just consuming cash and piling on debt; it’s also issuing more claims on whatever profits do emerge. AI stocks started really selling off just as it became clear that more equity issuance would be part of the buildout story."
